meta.name: Drug targets
meta.about: Biological targets: the receptors, enzymes, ion channels, transporters and pathways that medicines act on. Each page explains what the target does in the body, where it is found, which medicines and drug classes act on it and which physiology and conditions it connects to. The bridge between a medicine and the anatomy it changes.

l-type-calcium-channel.name: L-type calcium channel
l-type-calcium-channel.summary: A voltage-gated channel in the membrane of smooth-muscle and heart-muscle cells that lets calcium in when the cell is electrically excited. Calcium entry is what makes the muscle contract, so blocking the channel relaxes artery walls and, for some drugs, slows the heart.
l-type-calcium-channel.what: L-type ('long-lasting') calcium channels open when the membrane depolarises and stay open long enough for a substantial calcium current. In vascular smooth muscle the calcium that enters activates the contractile proteins directly, setting the tone of arterioles and therefore blood pressure. In heart muscle the same channel triggers a much larger release of calcium from internal stores with each beat, and in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes it carries the current that generates and conducts the heartbeat. The dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine) bind a site on the channel that is favoured in relaxed, depolarised vascular muscle, so they dilate arteries with little effect on the heart; verapamil and diltiazem bind differently and also slow the heart's nodes.
l-type-calcium-channel.role: Sets arteriolar tone (blood pressure), drives cardiac contraction and conduction through the AV node, and contributes to insulin release and neurotransmitter release elsewhere in the body.
l-type-calcium-channel.location: Cell membranes of vascular smooth muscle in arterioles and arteries, cardiac muscle and the heart's conduction tissue; also endocrine and nerve cells.

at1-receptor.name: Angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor
at1-receptor.summary: The receptor through which angiotensin II constricts arteries, releases aldosterone and drives the thickening of heart and vessel walls. Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, candesartan, valsartan) occupy it so that angiotensin II cannot act.
at1-receptor.what: Angiotensin II is the final product of the renin–angiotensin system, released whenever the kidney senses low pressure or low salt. Acting on AT1 receptors it narrows arterioles within seconds, prompts the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone (which makes the kidney retain salt and water), constricts the efferent arteriole of the glomerulus to hold up filtration pressure, stimulates thirst and sympathetic activity, and over months promotes growth and fibrosis in the heart, arteries and kidney. Blocking AT1 therefore lowers blood pressure, reduces the strain on a failing heart, lowers pressure inside the glomerulus (which protects diabetic kidneys but can drop filtration if the renal arteries are narrowed) and raises potassium by removing the aldosterone signal. ACE inhibitors act one step upstream by preventing angiotensin II from being made at all.
at1-receptor.role: Vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sodium and water retention, glomerular pressure control and long-term cardiovascular remodelling.
at1-receptor.location: Vascular smooth muscle, the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa), the kidney's afferent and efferent arterioles and tubules, the heart, the brain and the sympathetic nerve endings.

angiotensin-converting-enzyme.name: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.summary: The enzyme on the surface of blood-vessel lining cells, above all in the lungs, that converts inactive angiotensin I into angiotensin II and also breaks down bradykinin. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, ramipril) block it, lowering blood pressure and protecting the heart and kidneys.
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.what: Renin from the kidney clips angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, which is inactive until ACE removes two amino acids to make angiotensin II. ACE sits on endothelial cells throughout the circulation, most densely in the pulmonary capillaries, so a single pass through the lungs activates the hormone. The same enzyme inactivates bradykinin, a peptide that widens vessels and, in the airways, irritates cough receptors. Inhibiting ACE therefore lowers angiotensin II (less constriction, less aldosterone, lower glomerular pressure) and raises bradykinin (extra vasodilation, but also the dry cough that affects around one in ten people and the rare but dangerous swelling of angioedema). Because angiotensin II can still be made by other enzymes, ARBs that block the receptor itself are the alternative when the cough is intolerable.
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.role: Activation of the renin–angiotensin system (angiotensin II production) and inactivation of bradykinin.
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.location: The luminal surface of endothelial cells lining blood vessels, particularly the pulmonary capillaries; also kidney tubules, gut, brain and testis.

hmg-coa-reductase.name: HMG-CoA reductase
hmg-coa-reductase.summary: The enzyme that controls the speed of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. Statins block it, so liver cells make less cholesterol and pull more LDL out of the blood, lowering LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart attack and stroke.
hmg-coa-reductase.what: Cholesterol is built in a long chain of reactions, and the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate by HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting step and the point the cell regulates. Statins are close mimics of HMG-CoA that sit in the enzyme's active site. When synthesis falls, the liver cell senses low cholesterol and responds by displaying more LDL receptors on its surface, which capture LDL particles from the blood; that receptor response, more than the fall in synthesis itself, is what lowers LDL cholesterol by 30 to 55% depending on the statin and dose. The enzyme is present in every cell, but statins are taken up mostly by the liver, which is why their main effects and most of their side effects (including the rise in liver enzymes) relate to it. Muscle symptoms are thought to involve the same pathway in muscle cells.
hmg-coa-reductase.role: Rate-limiting step of cholesterol biosynthesis; its inhibition upregulates hepatic LDL receptors.
hmg-coa-reductase.location: The endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells (hepatocytes), and at lower levels in all nucleated cells.

cox-1.name: Cyclo-oxygenase 1 (COX-1)
cox-1.summary: The 'housekeeping' form of cyclo-oxygenase, present all the time in platelets, the stomach lining and the kidney. It makes the thromboxane that lets platelets clump and the prostaglandins that protect the stomach and keep the kidneys perfused; aspirin and other NSAIDs block it.
cox-1.what: Cyclo-oxygenases convert arachidonic acid released from cell membranes into the prostaglandins and thromboxane that act as short-range messengers. COX-1 is constitutive: it is always present and supplies the everyday prostaglandins that keep the stomach lining coated in mucus and bicarbonate, maintain blood flow through the kidney when the body is stressed, and, in platelets, make thromboxane A2, the signal that recruits other platelets to a clot. Low-dose aspirin acetylates COX-1 irreversibly; because platelets have no nucleus they cannot replace the enzyme, so a small daily dose suppresses thromboxane for the platelet's whole life. Non-selective NSAIDs such as ibuprofen block COX-1 reversibly, which explains their shared risks: stomach ulcers and bleeding, reduced kidney perfusion in the dehydrated, and a temporary antiplatelet effect that can interfere with aspirin's.
cox-1.role: Platelet aggregation (thromboxane A2), gastric mucosal protection and renal blood flow (prostaglandins).
cox-1.location: Platelets, the gastric and duodenal mucosa, the kidney and vascular endothelium; present in most tissues at a basal level.

cox-2.name: Cyclo-oxygenase 2 (COX-2)
cox-2.summary: The inducible form of cyclo-oxygenase, switched on at sites of injury and inflammation and in the brain during fever. Its prostaglandins sensitise pain nerves, widen inflamed vessels and reset the body's thermostat; NSAIDs relieve pain, swelling and fever by blocking it.
cox-2.what: COX-2 is barely present in most resting tissues but is induced within hours by cytokines and growth factors wherever tissue is damaged or inflamed, and in the hypothalamus in response to the pyrogens of infection. Its prostaglandins (mainly PGE2 and prostacyclin) lower the threshold of pain fibres, dilate vessels and increase their leakiness (redness, warmth, swelling), and raise the hypothalamic set-point that produces fever. Ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac block COX-2 and COX-1 together; celecoxib and etoricoxib block COX-2 selectively and spare the stomach, but because COX-2 also makes the prostacyclin that keeps the vessel lining anti-thrombotic (unlike platelet thromboxane, which is COX-1), selective inhibition tilts the balance towards clotting, the basis of the cardiovascular warnings on all NSAIDs. COX-2 is also constitutive in the kidney and in healing tissue, which is why NSAIDs can impair kidney function and delay ulcer healing.
cox-2.role: Inflammatory prostaglandin production: pain sensitisation, vasodilation and oedema in inflamed tissue, fever; vascular prostacyclin and renal prostaglandins.
cox-2.location: Induced in inflamed and injured tissue (joints, skin, gut, muscle), macrophages and the hypothalamus; constitutively present in the kidney, vascular endothelium and brain.

serotonin-transporter.name: Serotonin transporter (SERT)
serotonin-transporter.summary: The pump on the presynaptic nerve ending that clears serotonin from the synapse after it has been released. SSRIs such as sertraline block it, so serotonin stays in the synapse longer; the antidepressant effect follows over weeks as receptors and circuits adapt.
serotonin-transporter.what: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) released into a synapse acts on receptors on the next neuron and is then recycled by the serotonin transporter, a membrane protein that carries it back into the releasing nerve ending. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors bind the transporter and stop that recycling within hours of the first dose, yet mood improvement takes two to six weeks, which shows that the benefit comes from slower downstream changes in receptor sensitivity, gene expression and neural plasticity rather than from the raised serotonin itself. The same transporter is present on platelets, where blocking it depletes their serotonin and slightly impairs clotting (a reason bleeding risk rises when SSRIs are combined with NSAIDs or anticoagulants), and in the gut wall, where serotonin regulates motility (nausea and bowel changes early in treatment). Combining several serotonergic drugs can over-stimulate serotonin receptors and cause serotonin syndrome.
serotonin-transporter.role: Terminates serotonin signalling by reuptake into presynaptic neurons; also loads serotonin into platelets.
serotonin-transporter.location: Presynaptic membranes of serotonergic neurons originating in the brainstem raphe nuclei and projecting throughout the brain; platelet membranes; enterochromaffin cells and nerves of the gut wall.

beta-1-adrenoceptor.name: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor
beta-1-adrenoceptor.summary: The receptor in heart muscle and the heart's pacemaker tissue through which adrenaline and noradrenaline speed the heart and strengthen its contraction. Beta blockers occupy it to slow the heart, lower its oxygen demand and protect it after a heart attack and in heart failure.
beta-1-adrenoceptor.what: Sympathetic nerves and the adrenal medulla act on the heart through beta-1 receptors on the sinoatrial node (faster rate), the atrioventricular node (faster conduction) and the muscle of the atria and ventricles (stronger contraction and faster relaxation). Beta-1 receptors on the kidney's juxtaglomerular cells also release renin. Blocking them reduces heart rate and contractility, which cuts the heart's oxygen consumption (the basis of angina relief), suppresses abnormal rhythms, lowers blood pressure partly through less renin, and in chronic heart failure protects the myocardium from sustained sympathetic overdrive. Cardioselective beta blockers such as bisoprolol and metoprolol prefer beta-1 over the beta-2 receptors of the airways, though selectivity is relative and asthma remains a caution. Sudden withdrawal after long use can rebound with tachycardia and angina because the receptors have become more numerous.
beta-1-adrenoceptor.role: Increases heart rate, conduction velocity and contractility in response to catecholamines; stimulates renin release.
beta-1-adrenoceptor.location: Sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, atrial and ventricular myocardium, and the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney.

beta-2-adrenoceptor.name: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor
beta-2-adrenoceptor.summary: The receptor on airway smooth muscle through which adrenaline relaxes the bronchi. Salbutamol and other beta-2 agonists stimulate it to open the airways in asthma and COPD; non-selective beta blockers block it and can provoke bronchospasm.
beta-2-adrenoceptor.what: Beta-2 receptors respond mainly to circulating adrenaline rather than to direct nerve supply. In bronchial smooth muscle they raise cyclic AMP, which relaxes the muscle and widens the airway within minutes; they also increase mucociliary clearance and stabilise mast cells. In skeletal muscle they cause tremor and drive potassium into cells (high-dose salbutamol lowers blood potassium), in the liver they release glucose, in the uterus they relax the muscle, and in blood vessels supplying muscle they dilate. Short-acting agonists such as salbutamol act for about four hours as relievers; long-acting agonists (salmeterol, formoterol) last twelve hours or more and are combined with inhaled corticosteroids, because used alone in asthma they can mask worsening inflammation. Frequent use down-regulates the receptors, one reason reliever overuse signals poorly controlled asthma.
beta-2-adrenoceptor.role: Bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle, glycogen breakdown, uterine relaxation and potassium uptake into cells.
beta-2-adrenoceptor.location: Smooth muscle of the bronchi and bronchioles, vascular smooth muscle in skeletal muscle beds, the uterus, liver and skeletal muscle cells, and mast cells.

proton-pump.name: Gastric proton pump (H+/K+ ATPase)
proton-pump.summary: The enzyme in the stomach's parietal cells that pumps acid into the stomach as the final step of acid secretion. Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole disable it, cutting acid output by more than 90% and allowing ulcers and reflux oesophagitis to heal.
proton-pump.what: Parietal cells in the glands of the stomach body secrete hydrochloric acid by swapping potassium for hydrogen ions across their apical membrane using the H+/K+ ATPase, an energy-consuming pump that can create a million-fold concentration gradient. Histamine, gastrin and the vagus nerve each stimulate the cell through separate receptors, but all three converge on this pump, which is why blocking it suppresses acid more completely than blocking any one signal (H2 blockers such as famotidine block only the histamine route). Proton pump inhibitors are inactive prodrugs that concentrate in the acid canaliculus of the parietal cell, are converted there and bind the pump irreversibly; acid secretion only returns once new pumps are synthesised, so a once-daily dose taken before breakfast works around the clock. Long-term loss of acid raises gastrin, changes the gut flora and modestly reduces absorption of magnesium, vitamin B12, iron and calcium.
proton-pump.role: Final common step of gastric acid secretion.
proton-pump.location: The apical (canalicular) membrane of parietal cells in the oxyntic glands of the stomach body and fundus.

penicillin-binding-proteins.name: Penicillin-binding proteins
penicillin-binding-proteins.summary: Bacterial enzymes that cross-link the peptidoglycan mesh of the cell wall as bacteria grow. Penicillins, cephalosporins and other beta-lactam antibiotics bind them, the wall weakens and the bacterium bursts; human cells have no cell wall, so the drugs spare them.
penicillin-binding-proteins.what: The bacterial cell wall is a single giant molecule of peptidoglycan, sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides, that holds the cell together against its own high internal pressure. Penicillin-binding proteins are the transpeptidases that make those cross-links, and beta-lactam antibiotics mimic the natural substrate closely enough to bind the active site permanently. Growing bacteria with unfinished walls then lyse, which is why beta-lactams work best on actively dividing organisms and why they are bactericidal. Resistance arises when bacteria make beta-lactamase enzymes that destroy the drug (countered by clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav), alter their PBPs so the drug no longer binds (the mechanism of MRSA and penicillin-resistant pneumococci), or, in Gram-negative organisms, restrict entry through their outer membrane. Because the target does not exist in humans, side effects come from allergy and from disruption of the body's own bacterial flora rather than from the mechanism itself.
penicillin-binding-proteins.role: Synthesis and remodelling of bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan (transpeptidation).
penicillin-binding-proteins.location: The cytoplasmic membrane of bacteria, facing the cell wall; absent from human cells.

bacterial-ribosome.name: Bacterial ribosome (50S subunit)
bacterial-ribosome.summary: The protein-making machinery of bacteria, built differently enough from the human ribosome to be a selective drug target. Macrolides such as azithromycin bind the 50S subunit and stop the bacterium making proteins, halting its growth.
bacterial-ribosome.what: Every cell makes protein on ribosomes, but bacterial ribosomes (70S, made of 30S and 50S subunits) differ from human cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S) in their RNA and proteins, so antibiotics can bind them selectively. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) bind the 23S ribosomal RNA in the exit tunnel of the 50S subunit and block the growing peptide chain from leaving, which stops protein synthesis; the effect is mainly bacteriostatic, leaving the immune system to clear the organism. Because macrolides reach very high concentrations inside cells, they are effective against intracellular organisms such as Chlamydia, Mycoplasma and Legionella that penicillins cannot reach. Other classes target the ribosome at different sites: tetracyclines and aminoglycosides on the 30S subunit, clindamycin and linezolid on the 50S. Human mitochondria have ribosomes of bacterial ancestry, which may contribute to some antibiotic toxicities. Resistance follows methylation of the binding site or efflux pumps.
bacterial-ribosome.role: Bacterial protein synthesis (translation); inhibition halts bacterial growth.
bacterial-ribosome.location: The cytoplasm of bacteria; not present in human cytoplasm (mitochondrial ribosomes are related but distinct).

hepatic-glucose-production.name: Hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis)
hepatic-glucose-production.summary: The liver's manufacture and release of glucose between meals, from lactate, amino acids and glycerol. In type 2 diabetes this output runs too high; metformin's main action is to reduce it, which lowers fasting blood glucose without causing hypoglycaemia.
hepatic-glucose-production.what: Between meals and overnight the liver keeps blood glucose steady, first by releasing stored glycogen and then by making new glucose (gluconeogenesis) from lactate, alanine and glycerol. Insulin normally restrains this; in type 2 diabetes the liver is insulin-resistant and keeps producing glucose even when levels are already high, which is the main reason fasting glucose rises. Metformin accumulates in hepatocytes and lowers their energy state (through effects on mitochondrial respiration and the energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase, and on the redox balance that gluconeogenesis depends on), which switches gluconeogenesis down and modestly increases insulin sensitivity in muscle. Because it does not push the pancreas to release insulin, metformin does not cause low blood sugar on its own. The same reliance on mitochondrial function underlies its rare serious harm: when the drug accumulates in kidney failure or severe illness, lactate that the liver would normally convert to glucose builds up (lactic acidosis).
hepatic-glucose-production.role: Maintains blood glucose during fasting; excessive output drives fasting hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes.
hepatic-glucose-production.location: Hepatocytes, particularly those around the portal tracts; the kidney cortex contributes a smaller share.

mu-opioid-receptor.name: Mu-opioid receptor
mu-opioid-receptor.summary: The receptor through which morphine and the other opioids relieve pain, and also the one responsible for their sedation, slowed breathing, constipation, euphoria and dependence. The body's own endorphins act on the same receptor.
mu-opioid-receptor.what: Mu-opioid receptors sit on nerve cells in the spinal cord's dorsal horn, in the brainstem and midbrain, in the limbic system and in the gut wall. Activation reduces the release of pain transmitters in the spinal cord, switches on descending pathways from the brainstem that dampen pain signals, and changes how the pain is experienced in the brain, so the pain is still detected but matters less. The same receptors in the medulla blunt the response to rising carbon dioxide, which is why overdose kills by stopping breathing and why naloxone, which displaces opioids from the receptor, reverses it within minutes. In the gut they slow motility and tighten sphincters, causing the constipation that does not fade with time. Repeated stimulation leads to tolerance (more drug for the same effect) and physical dependence, with withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped abruptly. Codeine and tramadol are weaker or partial agonists; buprenorphine is a partial agonist used in dependence treatment.
mu-opioid-receptor.role: Analgesia, sedation, respiratory depression, reduced gut motility, euphoria and reward; tolerance and dependence with sustained use.
mu-opioid-receptor.location: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord, periaqueductal grey and medulla of the brainstem, thalamus, limbic system and the enteric nerves of the gut wall.

h1-receptor.name: Histamine H1 receptor
h1-receptor.summary: The receptor through which histamine, released from mast cells in an allergic reaction, causes itching, sneezing, a runny nose, swelling and hives. Antihistamines such as cetirizine block it; older antihistamines also reach H1 receptors in the brain and cause drowsiness.
h1-receptor.what: When an allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells in the skin, nose, airways or gut, the cells release histamine within minutes. Acting on H1 receptors, histamine widens small vessels and makes them leak (redness and swelling, the wheal of a hive), stimulates itch and pain nerve endings, contracts bronchial and gut smooth muscle and increases mucus secretion. H1 antagonists compete for the receptor (technically as inverse agonists) and relieve the itch, sneezing and rhinorrhoea of hay fever and urticaria, but they do little for the airway narrowing of asthma, which involves many other mediators. First-generation antihistamines (chlorphenamine, promethazine) cross the blood–brain barrier, where H1 receptors help maintain wakefulness, so they sedate and impair driving; second-generation drugs (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) are kept out of the brain by transporters and cause far less drowsiness. Histamine's other receptors do different jobs: H2 drives stomach acid, H3 and H4 modulate nerves and immune cells.
h1-receptor.role: Mediates the acute allergic response (vasodilation, vascular leak, itch, bronchoconstriction, mucus) and contributes to wakefulness in the brain.
h1-receptor.location: Endothelium and smooth muscle of small blood vessels, sensory nerve endings in the skin and mucosa, bronchial and gut smooth muscle, and neurons in the brain.

vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.name: Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1)
vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.summary: The liver enzyme that recycles vitamin K so it can activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Warfarin blocks it, so the liver releases inactive clotting factors and blood clots more slowly; the effect builds over days and is measured with the INR.
vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.what: Four clotting factors and two anticoagulant proteins (C and S) are only functional after a vitamin K-dependent step that adds carboxyl groups to them; each cycle oxidises vitamin K, and VKORC1 reduces it back for reuse. Warfarin inhibits VKORC1, vitamin K becomes unavailable, and newly made factors are released as inactive precursors. Because circulating factors are only replaced as they decay (factor VII within hours, prothrombin over two to three days), anticoagulation takes several days to develop and heparin cover is used at the start; the temporary early fall of protein C can even make clotting worse briefly. The dose needed varies many-fold between people, partly because of common variants in the VKORC1 and CYP2C9 genes, and it is disturbed by dietary vitamin K (green vegetables), alcohol, illness and a very long list of interacting drugs, hence the need for regular INR monitoring. Vitamin K itself, given by mouth or injection, reverses warfarin over hours; clotting factor concentrates do so immediately.
vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.role: Regeneration of reduced vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S.

factor-xa.name: Factor Xa
factor-xa.summary: The clotting enzyme at the junction of the two arms of the coagulation cascade, which converts prothrombin into thrombin. Apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban block it directly, preventing clots in atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism without the monitoring warfarin needs.
factor-xa.what: Coagulation proceeds as a chain of enzyme activations that all converge on factor X. Once activated to factor Xa, it assembles with factor Va on the surface of platelets to form the prothrombinase complex, which generates thrombin, and thrombin then converts fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh of a clot and amplifies its own production. Each molecule of Xa yields many molecules of thrombin, so blocking Xa is an efficient way to reduce clotting. Direct oral anticoagulants bind the active site of Xa reversibly, take effect within hours, and have predictable dosing that does not require INR checks, although kidney function, body weight and interacting drugs (strong inhibitors or inducers of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein) affect their levels. Low-molecular-weight heparins such as enoxaparin inhibit Xa indirectly through antithrombin. Andexanet alfa is a specific reversal agent; bleeding is the shared main risk of every drug in this pathway, and it multiplies when they are combined with antiplatelets or NSAIDs.
factor-xa.role: Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, the amplifying step of the coagulation cascade.
factor-xa.location: Circulating in plasma as inactive factor X; activated on the surface of platelets and damaged endothelium at the site of injury.

nkcc2.name: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2)
nkcc2.summary: The transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle that reabsorbs sodium, potassium and chloride from the filtrate. Loop diuretics such as furosemide block it, so the kidney passes far more salt and water, relieving the fluid overload of heart failure.
nkcc2.what: About a quarter of the sodium the kidney filters is reclaimed in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle by NKCC2, which carries one sodium, one potassium and two chloride ions together from the tubular fluid into the cell. Because this segment is impermeable to water, the salt it removes also builds the concentration gradient in the kidney medulla that later allows urine to be concentrated. Loop diuretics reach the transporter from the tubular side (they are secreted into the tubule by the proximal cells, so they still work when filtration is poor) and block it; salt that stays in the tubule drags water with it, the medullary gradient collapses, and a large, dilute diuresis follows within an hour of a dose. The lost potassium, magnesium and calcium explain the electrolyte disturbances of loop diuretics, the fall in blood volume explains dizziness and rising creatinine, and the same transporter in the inner ear accounts for their rare ototoxicity at high doses. NSAIDs blunt the effect by reducing the prostaglandins that support it.
nkcc2.role: Reabsorbs about 25% of filtered sodium and chloride and generates the medullary concentration gradient; also reabsorbs potassium, calcium and magnesium indirectly.
nkcc2.location: Apical membrane of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the kidney; a related isoform is in the inner ear.

xanthine-oxidase.name: Xanthine oxidase
xanthine-oxidase.summary: The enzyme that makes uric acid from the purines released when cells and DNA break down. Allopurinol and febuxostat block it, lowering uric acid so that the crystals of gout dissolve and new attacks stop.
xanthine-oxidase.what: Purines from the diet and from the turnover of the body's own cells are degraded to hypoxanthine and xanthine, and xanthine oxidase converts both, in two steps, to uric acid. Humans lack the enzyme most mammals use to break uric acid down further, so blood levels sit close to the point at which urate crystals form, especially in cool joints such as the big toe. Allopurinol, a purine analogue, is itself converted by xanthine oxidase into oxypurinol, which inhibits the enzyme for the whole day; febuxostat inhibits it non-competitively. Both lower serum urate within days, but dissolving existing crystals takes months, during which attacks can be provoked, so treatment is started low, raised gradually against the urate level and covered with an anti-inflammatory. Xanthine oxidase also metabolises azathioprine and mercaptopurine, so inhibiting it can raise those drugs to dangerous levels; the enzyme's production of reactive oxygen species links it to tissue injury after ischaemia.
xanthine-oxidase.role: Final steps of purine catabolism to uric acid; a source of reactive oxygen species.
xanthine-oxidase.location: The cytoplasm of liver and gut cells, and vascular endothelium; also present in milk and the mammary gland.

glucocorticoid-receptor.name: Glucocorticoid receptor
glucocorticoid-receptor.summary: The receptor inside almost every cell through which cortisol, and corticosteroid medicines such as prednisolone and inhaled beclometasone, switch inflammatory genes off and metabolic genes on. It gives steroids their power against inflammation and also their long list of side effects.
glucocorticoid-receptor.what: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex, and synthetic glucocorticoids, pass through the cell membrane and bind the glucocorticoid receptor waiting in the cytoplasm. The complex moves into the nucleus, where it suppresses the transcription factors that drive inflammatory genes (cytokines, adhesion molecules, COX-2) and activates genes for anti-inflammatory proteins, gluconeogenesis and protein breakdown. The anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects are used in asthma, COPD flares, inflammatory arthritis, bowel disease, allergic reactions and transplant medicine; the metabolic effects produce the side effects of systemic treatment: raised blood glucose, muscle and skin thinning, bone loss, weight gain, mood change, high blood pressure and infection risk. Inhaled and topical steroids reach high concentrations at the target with little systemic exposure. Because the pituitary shuts down its own ACTH when circulating steroid is high, the adrenal glands shrink during prolonged courses, and stopping abruptly can precipitate adrenal crisis; doses are tapered.
glucocorticoid-receptor.role: Regulates transcription of inflammatory, immune and metabolic genes; mediates the stress response.
glucocorticoid-receptor.location: Cytoplasm and nucleus of nearly all cells, with the strongest effects in immune cells, airway and skin, liver, muscle, bone, fat and the hypothalamus–pituitary axis.

thyroid-hormone-receptor.name: Thyroid hormone receptor
thyroid-hormone-receptor.summary: The nuclear receptor in nearly every cell through which triiodothyronine (T3) sets the pace of metabolism, heart rate, temperature and growth. Levothyroxine replaces the thyroid's output and acts on it after conversion to T3.
thyroid-hormone-receptor.what: The thyroid secretes mostly thyroxine (T4), which tissues convert to the active hormone T3 with deiodinase enzymes; T3 enters the nucleus and binds thyroid hormone receptors that switch genes on or off. In the heart the result is a faster rate and stronger contraction, in metabolism a higher resting energy expenditure and heat production, in the liver lower cholesterol, in bone higher turnover, and in the developing brain normal maturation, which is why newborns are screened for hypothyroidism. Levothyroxine is synthetic T4: taken once daily on an empty stomach it is converted to T3 as the body requires, giving steady levels with a half-life of about a week. Dosing is judged by the TSH, which the pituitary lowers as replacement becomes adequate. Too much replacement drives the same receptors excessively and causes palpitations, atrial fibrillation, weight loss, anxiety and bone loss; too little leaves the tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance and slowed heart of hypothyroidism. Iron, calcium, antacids and proton pump inhibitors cut absorption of the tablet.
thyroid-hormone-receptor.role: Transcriptional control of metabolic rate, cardiac output, thermogenesis, lipid metabolism, growth and neurodevelopment.
thyroid-hormone-receptor.location: Nuclei of cells in virtually all tissues, with distinct receptor subtypes dominant in heart, brain, liver and pituitary.

insulin-receptor.name: Insulin receptor
insulin-receptor.summary: The receptor on muscle, fat and liver cells through which insulin moves glucose out of the blood and into storage. Insulin injections act on it directly in type 1 diabetes; in type 2 diabetes the receptor's signalling is blunted (insulin resistance) and metformin helps restore the response.
insulin-receptor.what: Insulin from the pancreatic beta cells binds the outer part of its receptor, a tyrosine kinase that spans the cell membrane, and the receptor phosphorylates itself and a chain of signalling proteins inside the cell. In muscle and fat the signal brings GLUT4 glucose transporters to the cell surface, so glucose floods in and is burned or stored as glycogen and fat; in the liver it switches off glucose production and switches on glycogen and fat synthesis; in all tissues it promotes protein synthesis and blocks the breakdown of fat. In type 1 diabetes the beta cells are destroyed and injected insulin, in rapid- and long-acting forms, replaces the hormone; in type 2 diabetes the receptors are present but the signal is dampened by excess fat inside cells and by inflammation, so the pancreas overproduces insulin until it can no longer keep up. Weight loss, exercise and metformin improve the receptor response; sulfonylureas and GLP-1 agonists increase insulin supply. The main danger of insulin treatment is hypoglycaemia when the dose exceeds the food and activity of the day.
insulin-receptor.role: Uptake and storage of glucose, suppression of hepatic glucose output, promotion of protein and fat synthesis; growth signalling.
insulin-receptor.location: Cell membranes of skeletal muscle, fat, liver and most other tissues, including the brain.

androgen-receptor.name: Androgen receptor
androgen-receptor.summary: The nuclear receptor through which testosterone and dihydrotestosterone act on the genitals, prostate, muscle, bone, bone marrow, skin, hair and brain. Testosterone treatment for hypogonadism and masculinising gender-affirming therapy act through it; anti-androgens block it in feminising therapy and in prostate cancer.
androgen-receptor.what: Testosterone, made by the Leydig cells of the testes and in smaller amounts by the ovaries and adrenal glands, crosses into cells and binds the androgen receptor in the nucleus; in the prostate, skin and hair follicles it is first converted by 5-alpha-reductase to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which binds the receptor more tightly. The bound receptor attaches to androgen response elements in DNA and changes which genes are transcribed over hours to days. Before birth testosterone acting on this receptor forms the internal male ducts and, as DHT, the prostate and external genitalia. At puberty and afterwards it drives growth of the testes, penis and larynx, sperm production, muscle, bone density, red cell production in the marrow, sebum, beard and body hair, and libido. In women it mediates the smaller amounts of androgen from the ovaries and adrenals acting on libido, muscle and bone, and its overstimulation in polycystic ovary syndrome produces hirsutism and acne; DHT on scalp follicles causes male-pattern hair loss. Testosterone given for hypogonadism or masculinising therapy is a full agonist and produces the same changes in trans men and non-binary people. Anti-androgens block the receptor: cyproterone acetate and spironolactone in feminising therapy, bicalutamide in prostate cancer, which grows through this receptor; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride cut DHT production.
androgen-receptor.role: Male development of the internal and external genitalia before birth, puberty and spermatogenesis, and lifelong maintenance of muscle mass, bone density, red cell production, sebum and hair growth, libido and prostate size.
androgen-receptor.location: Nuclei of cells in the prostate, seminal vesicles, testes (Sertoli and Leydig cells), penis and clitoris, skeletal muscle, bone, bone marrow, sebaceous glands and hair follicles, larynx, hypothalamus and brain, ovarian theca cells and the adrenal glands.

oestrogen-receptor.name: Oestrogen receptor
oestrogen-receptor.summary: The nuclear receptor through which oestradiol acts on the uterus, breast, bone, blood vessels, liver and brain. Estradiol replacement, hormone replacement therapy and feminising hormone therapy act through it, and most breast cancers carry it, which is why ER status is tested on every breast cancer and ER-positive tumours are treated with endocrine therapy.
oestrogen-receptor.what: Oestradiol, the main oestrogen, is a lipid-soluble steroid that crosses the cell membrane and binds oestrogen receptors in the nucleus. The bound receptor pairs up, attaches to oestrogen response elements in DNA and recruits co-activators or co-repressors, switching genes on or off over hours to days. In the uterus oestradiol makes the endometrium proliferate and induces progesterone receptors in it; in the breast it grows the ducts; in bone it restrains osteoclasts and, at puberty, fuses the growth plates in girls and boys alike (boys make the oestradiol from testosterone with aromatase); in the liver it raises binding proteins and clotting factors and shifts cholesterol towards HDL; in vessels it promotes dilation; and in the hypothalamus it feeds back on GnRH and steadies the temperature-regulating centre, which is why its withdrawal at the menopause brings hot flushes, bone loss and vaginal thinning. Estradiol given as HRT or feminising therapy is a full agonist at the receptor. Tamoxifen and raloxifene are selective modulators that block it in the breast while stimulating it in bone, and aromatase inhibitors starve it of ligand. Most breast cancers express the receptor and grow in response to oestrogen, so ER status is measured on every breast cancer biopsy and ER-positive tumours are treated with endocrine therapy. Endometriosis and fibroids are likewise oestrogen-dependent and regress after the menopause.
oestrogen-receptor.role: Transcriptional control of the endometrium and menstrual cycle, breast development, bone density and growth plate closure in both sexes, vascular tone and lipid metabolism, hypothalamic feedback and temperature regulation.
oestrogen-receptor.location: Nuclei of cells in the endometrium and myometrium, breast ducts and lobules, ovarian granulosa cells, bone, liver, blood vessel walls, fat, hypothalamus and pituitary, and in men the testes and prostate; ERα predominates in uterus, breast, liver and bone, ERβ in ovary, prostate, lung and brain.
